government.note: Government type as on 1 January 2000: Ba'athist Iraq. Saddam Hussein was President (since 16 July 1979), Chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council, Prime Minister (since 29 May 1994) and Regional Secretary of the Ba'ath Party, which led the National Progressive Front. Candidates for the National Assembly were approved in advance. The Kurdish north (KUR) had been outside Baghdad's control since 1991. Stages after 2000, as dated facts: the government fell when US forces took Baghdad on 9 April 2003; Jay Garner directed the Office for Reconstruction and Humanitarian Assistance from 21 April 2003; Paul Bremer headed the Coalition Provisional Authority from 12 May 2003 to 28 June 2004; an appointed Iraqi Governing Council sat from 13 July 2003 to 1 June 2004 under a monthly rotating presidency; the Iraqi Interim Government (President Ghazi al-Yawer, Prime Minister Ayad Allawi) took office on 1 June 2004 and sovereignty was transferred on 28 June 2004; a Transitional National Assembly was elected on 30 January 2005 and the Transitional Government of Ibrahim al-Jaafari took office on 3 May 2005; the permanent constitution was approved by referendum on 15 October 2005 and the first Council of Representatives was elected on 15 December 2005. Under the 2005 constitution Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic: the Council of Representatives elects the President, who charges the nominee of the largest bloc with forming a government. The type field keeps the 2000 value; from 2004-2005 the Prime Minister is the effective executive and the presidency is largely ceremonial.

offices.note: Before 2003 the President, as Chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council, held supreme executive power (power_weight reflects 2000). Under the 2005 constitution the presidency is primarily symbolic and the President is elected by the Council of Representatives for a four-year term; by the informal muhasasa convention it is held by a Kurd, and every President since 2005 has come from the PUK.

system.note: 2000: the National Assembly had 250 seats; candidates were approved beforehand by a committee chaired by the Justice Minister, and 30 members were appointed by the government to represent the Kurdish governorates outside its control. seats_2000 is the result of the 24 March 1996 election (the 27 March 2000 election gave the Ba'ath Party 165, independents 55 and 30 appointees). From 2005 the chamber was elected by list PR: 275 seats in 2005, 325 in 2010, 328 in 2014 and 329 from 2018. The 2025 infobox records 9 minority seats (also 9 in 2021). The seat count here is the 2000 figure; election records give the later sizes. District arrangements changed between elections and are not modelled.

chambers.review_note: The 1996 table gives Ba'ath 161, a 'Kurdistan Democratic Party' 3 (linked to Barzani's KDP, but probably a Baghdad-aligned group; recorded under others), Kurdistan Revolutionary Party 2, a Communist Party 1 and independents 83, totalling 250, while the text says 30 members were appointed for Kurdistan; it is unclear whether the appointees are counted among the independents.

start_2000.ideology_support_note: Estimate only: Ba'athist Iraq held no competitive elections (all 1996 and 2000 candidates were pre-approved, and the 2002 referendum reported 100% for Saddam Hussein), so there is no vote share to derive from. Weights are a gameplay estimate informed by the first free election, January 2005 (United Iraqi Alliance of Shia Islamist parties 48.2%, Kurdish alliance 25.7%, Allawi's secular Iraqi List 13.8%), adjusted for the 2000 situation, in which the Kurdish north (KUR) is a separate tag and the Ba'ath Party controlled public life: baathist = Ba'ath Party and its National Progressive Front partners; islamist = Shia Islamist opposition (Dawa, SCIRI) and Sunni Islamist currents; shia_theocratic = supporters of clerical rule; islamic_democrat = Iraqi Islamic Party; regionalist and social_democrat = Kurdish parties (KDP, PUK) among Kurds under Baghdad's control; marxist_leninist = Iraqi Communist Party; centrist_liberal / classical_liberal = Iraqi National Accord and Iraqi National Congress (exile opposition); tribal_traditional = tribal networks.

claims.note: Iraq regards the Kurdish governorates (Erbil, Dohuk, Sulaymaniyah) as part of its territory; they had been outside the central government's control since 1991. The 2005 constitution recognises the Kurdistan Region as a federal region of Iraq.
